name: Edwin Walker
role: United States Army major general and segregationist political activist
summary: Walker opposed racial integration and advocated militant resistance to communism and United Nations influence over American policy. His Texas campaign emphasized states’ rights, property protection, right-to-work legislation and limited taxation; his later writings alleged covert coordination among political and religious leaders.

decide-locally.rationale: His platform opposed federal intervention in education, welfare, business and labor and defended local civic responsibility.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: He opposed the federal intervention enforcing Black students’ access to formerly segregated educational institutions.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: His anti-UN campaign rejected international control over American forces and portrayed the organization as a threat to national survival.

nation-first.rationale: He framed the choice between national control and UN influence as a question of preserving American independence and traditions.

separate-church-state.rationale: No stated position on separating church and state; defending religious belief and speech as constitutionally protected is something nearby.

taxation-theft.rationale: He described taxation as an evil made necessary by government, advocating a minimum burden rather than declaring all taxation illegitimate.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: He organized resistance to the admission of a Black student to the segregated University of Mississippi and repudiated his earlier integration assignment.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: He alleges that national officials and religious leaders secretly coordinate policy and conceal the true purposes of wars and political events.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His opposition to Black admission to an all-white public university denies equal educational rights; no broader theory of human worth is assumed.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: His 1962 protest denounced the Supreme Court’s removal of school prayer as a betrayal of the nation.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: His later pamphlet condemns political briefings of clergy and describes churches subordinated to state direction as a feature of police states.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: He invokes constitutional protections of personal religious belief and speech against alleged coordination between state and clergy.

non-intervention.rationale: He advocated using American military force to remove communist rule in Cuba rather than respecting its internal political order.

defeat-communism.rationale: He rejected postwar policy as collaboration with an international communist conspiracy and campaigned for a more confrontational response.

property-franchise.rationale: He defended retaining the poll tax as a qualification that screened voters for willingness to accept civic responsibility.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: His March 1963 speech called for American military action to eliminate the communist regime in Cuba.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: His campaign platform promised a right-to-work guarantee alongside protection of citizens’ property.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: He pledged to work toward eliminating the need for a sales tax, favoring spending reductions over introducing or raising it.

no-business-privileges.rationale: His platform promised to remove special privilege, scandal and corruption from Texas government.

notes: No inferred answers. His execution of integration orders at Little Rock is distinguished from his own subsequent rejection of that assignment and his activism against integration at Oxford. Accounts that he personally led a physical charge were contested in libel litigation; no answer assumes that allegation proven. His sexual conduct and arrests do not establish views on same-sex marriage or criminalization. Associates’ positions, hostile fiction and undigitized archival holdings are not attributed to him. Full downloaded contemporary campaign coverage and the seven-page National Archives file were searched across themes; the scanned file was OCRed and its signed separation-of-church-and-state letter visually checked. No reliable position was found on most ecology, technology or detailed welfare questions. Reviewed all remaining null statements before finalization. Opposition to federal integration does not establish a specific racial franchise, genetic theory or immigration policy. The UN catalogue synopsis supplies only medium-confidence evidence; the recording itself was not transcribed. The militia, gun and racial claims of Arch Roberts in later journalism were not attributed to Walker.
